name: Gusztáv Sebes
scopeNote: Hungary national team coach, 1949 to 3 June 1956 (sacked after the 5-4 defeat to Belgium on 3 June 1956, per Wikipedia). The start is given as the year only: sources say he was in sole charge by 1949 and was described as 'recently appointed' in April 1949 (UEFA), but no appointment day was found. The Wikipedia infobox gives 1949-1957 while its managers list gives 1949-56; the 1956 end is used. Style: the evidence supports a radical variation of the WM formation (UEFA) that became the 4-2-4 shape with Nándor Hidegkuti as a deep-lying centre-forward (Wikipedia, UEFA, FIFA). The label 'socialist football' is Sebes's own term (FIFA, undated). Sources disagree on the shape label (2-3-3-2 in UEFA, 3-2-5 in other sources) and on who first used the 4-2-4 (Bukovi at MTK per some sources; Sebes, Guttmann and Bukovi as a 'triumvirate' per Wikipedia). Club coaching (Honvéd, Újpest, Diósgyőr) is not dated in the pages read and is excluded.

spellsCounted.reason: Built the Golden Team and the Hungarian 4-2-4 that won the 1952 Olympics and reached the 1954 World Cup final; the spell the profile is about.

openQuestions: The exact day of Sebes's appointment as sole national coach (1949) was not found.
The 4-2-4 label: UEFA describes a 2-3-3-2 lineup, other sources a 3-2-5 in practice; the shape should be checked against a match-line-up source.
Who first used the 4-2-4 (Márton Bukovi at MTK per some sources, Sebes as one of three pioneers per Wikipedia) should be settled before the ideology profile cites Sebes as its originator.
No primary Sebes interview on the system was found; the 'socialist football' quote is undated in the FIFA page read.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes - Wikipedia
sources.evidence: "He also made the decision to use Nándor Hidegkuti instead of Péter Palotás in the deep lying centre-forward role." Against Switzerland, 19 September 1952 (Central European Cup), Hungary was 2-0 down after half an hour; Hidegkuti replaced Palotás and Hungary won 4-2.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes - Wikipedia
sources.evidence: "He borrowed the heavier type of balls used by the English FA so that his team could practice with them." The article also says he changed the training pitch to match Wembley's dimensions, in the build-up to the 1953 match in England.

sources.title: The greatest teams of all time: Hungary 1950-56 - UEFA.com
sources.evidence: "Recently appointed coach Gusztáv Sebes did away with the established stars" (after the 5-2 defeat to Czechoslovakia in April 1949, which the page calls "a watershed moment").

sources.title: The greatest teams of all time: Hungary 1950-56 - UEFA.com
sources.evidence: "Sebes pioneered a radical variation of the WM formation" (the page covers the 1950-56 side; no single date given).

sources.evidence: "A deep-lying centre-forward, Hidegkuti used to draw defenders out of position and create space for Puskás and Kocsis." (the page covers the 1950-56 side; no single date given).

sources.title: The greatest teams of all time: Hungary 1950-56 - UEFA.com
sources.evidence: "Tactical discussions were regular, lengthy and usually included input from captain Puskás" (the page covers the 1950-56 side; no single date given).

sources.title: The beginning of the Magyars' magic - FIFA (inside.fifa.com)
sources.evidence: "socialist football": the page says Sebes described the team's intricate, cohesive style with this term. Undated in the page read; kept as context only.

sources.evidence: Puskás on Hidegkuti: "sitting at the front of the midfield" (undated in the page read; the page describes Hidegkuti as the attacking playmaker of Sebes's system). Kept as context only.

confidence.reason: Short evidence base: about 3 pages read, all tier C (Wikipedia, UEFA, FIFA), with one dated shape fact (1952 Hidegkuti switch) and the rest of the verified facts undated to the period. No tier A-B tactical analysis of Sebes's Hungary was found, and no primary Sebes interview on the system.
